sections.heading: Organizational Structure and Growth Strategy
sections.content: The company is restructuring its leadership to support rapid growth and operational scale, aiming for a turnover of 8 to 10 billion dirhams with clear delivery and strategy roles (00:00). Centralized Divisional Model with Delivery Focus (01:55) Portfolio managers oversee about five projects each, targeting 1.5 to 2 billion dirhams annually in turnover. Each project has dedicated commercial and project delivery teams with limited overhead support. Central functions like procurement, engineering, and HR remain centralized to optimize efficiency. New divisions, like MEP, are scaling rapidly aiming for 600 million dirhams turnover by year-end. Expansion Into New Geographic Markets (19:17) Plans to enter Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Eastern Europe within 24 months to diversify revenue sources. Uncertainty remains whether C-suite roles will become regional or replicate locally. Strategy depends on Dubai revenue trends, with potential for regional travel and backfilling roles accordingly. Expansion driven by infrastructure growth projections and large-scale urban development plans. Revenue and Market Positioning Insights (16:57) Focus on stable government clients like Aldar, Emar, and DHRE, avoiding new developers lacking track record. Emaar’s performance cited with sales of 87 billion dirhams and 23 billion dirhams net margin last year. Emphasis on maintaining high-quality reputation despite some market concerns about recent product quality. Growth fueled by government-backed projects to ensure steady pipeline despite market uncertainties. Growth-Driven Leadership and Structural Changes (01:08:03) Recent formalization of C-suite roles including CEO of Duco Construction and DBB to improve clarity and accountability. Current leadership structure transitioning from general managers to directors and executives aligned with scale. Goal to keep overheads below 3%, ideally closer to 2.25%, to maintain profitability as business grows. Two immediate C-suite hires planned to support delivery and strategy; others deferred until revenue reaches higher targets.

sections.heading: Talent Acquisition and Leadership Development
sections.content: The company seeks mature, credible leaders to manage rapid growth, focusing on attitude, experience, and emotional intelligence over formal qualifications (26:08). Key Leadership Roles Defined: Delivery and Strategy (14:18) Delivery role responsible for managing project portfolios up to 10 billion dirhams, ensuring margin and risk management. Strategy role responsible for centralized functions including HSE, design, business excellence, PMO, logistics, and quality. Both roles require strong people management skills, ability to drive discipline, and operational control. Expected salary range between 100,000 and 120,000 dirhams base with typical 60/40 basic-to-allowance split. Internal Succession Challenges and External Hiring Needs (20:30) Internal candidates like Daniel Potts and Johan acknowledged as experienced but not yet ready for expanded C-suite roles. No suitable internal candidate identified for the centralized strategy role; external search prioritized. Leadership acknowledges risks of promoting too early and is open to giving internal candidates development opportunities over time. Immediate hires targeted for Q3 due to expected project awards and workload increase. Desired Leadership Qualities and Cultural Fit (27:16) Preference for leaders with high emotional intelligence, humility, and ability to foster accountability and support. Emphasis on managing people and relationships rather than technical micro-management. Leader credibility critical to gain respect from experienced divisional managers and field teams. Culture emphasizes transparency, accountability, support, and a high-performance mindset with profit-sharing incentives. Diversity and Inclusion Considerations (34:50) Current leadership skewed towards Western backgrounds; company aims to increase gender and cultural diversity. Open to cosmopolitan candidates who bring varied perspectives and challenge the status quo. Recognition that diverse leadership improves problem solving and innovation in a growing enterprise. Hiring processes designed to minimize bias and focus on competencies and attitude.

sections.heading: Operational Discipline and Risk Management
sections.content: The company is tightening governance, risk management, and operational controls to stabilize growth and maintain profitability amid market challenges (59:32). Current Margin and Risk Environment (59:32) Main contracting margins range from 8 to 12% gross, with overheads not exceeding 3% typically. Market conditions have forced a flexible approach to processes to secure growth and projects. Leadership is uncomfortable with current laxity and aims to restore discipline and tighten controls in 2024. Emphasis on balancing opportunity realization with risk avoidance and maintaining sustainable margins. Data-Driven Performance and Accountability (01:01:53) Monthly risk and opportunity assessments show only 27% realization of forecasted opportunities historically. Leadership demands transparent tracking of performance against projections to identify recurring issues. Business lacks structured lessons learned processes; intent is to document mistakes to improve future outcomes. Focus on improving forecasting accuracy and operational decision making to avoid repeated losses. Governance and Reporting Enhancements (01:04:43) Introduction of ERP system via Oracle with 10 to 12 million dirhams investment to improve process flows. Establishment of clear delegation of authority and decision-making hierarchies across functions. Quarterly reviews and reporting structures designed to provide board with timely, accurate project status and financial data. Goal to create a best-practice, sustainable business model ready to withstand market downturns. Operational Challenges and Solutions (48:33) Current workforce includes 1,800 staff and 4,500 operatives, expected to grow to 2,500 staff and 10,000-12,000 operatives by year-end. Worker welfare and HR functions undergoing transformation, splitting compliance from people and culture roles. Onboarding and administrative processes are underdeveloped, requiring at least another year to stabilize fully. Leadership investing in learning and development to address operational gaps and support sustained growth.

sections.heading: Strategic Business Development and Market Positioning
sections.content: The company prioritizes stable government contracts and long-term partnerships to secure a solid project backlog and future growth (25:06). Robust Project Pipeline and Revenue Forecasts (25:06) Expected to win between 10 and 12 billion dirhams in new projects within the next three months. Backlog aimed to sustain 6 to 8 billion dirhams annually over the next three years. Focus remains on securing government and tier-one developer contracts to minimize market risk. Diversification into logistics, data centers, and other sectors planned to reduce reliance on residential markets. Long-Term Vision for Business Sustainability (01:05:51) Strategic planning includes potential IPO and geographic diversification to maintain growth momentum. C-suite roles structured to support governance, quarterly reviews, and scalable operational control. Emphasis on building a brand recognized for reliability, quality, and timely delivery to enhance market reputation. Leadership aims to balance aggressive growth with risk mitigation to protect margins and shareholder value. Manufacturing and Joint Venture Initiatives (06:46) Approved 120 million dirhams investment for a rebar manufacturing facility, though CAPEX deployment is delayed. Advanced joint ventures underway for precast concrete and modular building manufacturing involving Chinese partners. Plans to acquire a concrete manufacturing company to vertically integrate supply chain and improve margins. Manufacturing investments expected to enhance operational independence and reduce reliance on external suppliers. Minimal Business Development Function (42:48) Company does not have a dedicated business development director; most work sourced via group procurement and existing relationships. Estimation and bidding processes centralized under group chief procurement officer with technical support from PMO. Business development in interiors supported by a small creative design studio focused on niche markets. Strategy leverages long-standing reputation and family network rather than active external sales efforts.

summary_bullets: Market Expansion: Successfully entered Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Abu Dhabi, focusing on civil construction products and sustainable growth.
Workforce Shift: Approximately 80% of workforce (5,000 employees) moved to Abu Dhabi, providing a 5-7 year project pipeline.
Client Philosophy: Emphasizes quality and trust over volume, specializing in civil infrastructure to ensure project success and client satisfaction.
Worker Welfare Recognition: Awarded for worker safety initiatives, highlighting the commitment to well-being and operational excellence.
Leadership Development: Plans to launch a podcast series to share authentic leadership stories and foster industry engagement.

preferred_summary:
Middle East Market Expansion and Strategic Positioning: The company has strategically expanded into Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Abu Dhabi with a focused, controlled approach prioritizing core competencies and sustainable growth (04:35). Aaron Hennessy explained that after 10 years of preparation, they simultaneously established operations in Saudi Arabia and Abu Dhabi to "get the headache over as quickly as possible" (05:51). The entry targeted civil construction products only, avoiding speculative mega projects to maintain focus and quality. Initial contracts were secured immediately through existing EPC relationships, including work with Technicas Renitas, GA Cinema, and Petrofect, emphasizing trusted partnerships. The approach favors subcontracting roles under $1 billion, with a preference to start smaller (e.g., $100 million) to manage risk and learn site specifics before scaling up (08:54). This method fosters deep embedding with clients, ensuring higher quality and more frequent payments, which contrasts with chasing large, risky contracts. In terms of market differences, Aaron highlighted Oman’s slower decision-making culture and contractor mindset compared to Saudi and Abu Dhabi, where they found operations more aligned with their model (17:14). Saudi faces challenges like limited talent, infrastructure gaps, and aggressive project deadlines, making it a tougher environment to scale quickly (19:09). Operationally, logistics and labor laws are similar across Oman, Saudi, and UAE, allowing remote work and consistent processes despite geographic distances (20:47). The company has shifted about 80% of its workforce (around 5,000 people) and resources to Abu Dhabi, where project visibility and pipeline extend 5 to 7 years, compared to a less predictable outlook in Oman and Saudi (26:58). Abu Dhabi accounts for the majority of current work, followed by Saudi and then Oman, reflecting strategic prioritization based on market maturity and opportunities. This shift aligns with a nomadic business model ready to pivot as market conditions evolve.

Operational Excellence and Client Relationship Philosophy: The company maintains a disciplined focus on quality, trust, and long-term client relationships over chasing volume or speculative growth (06:00). Aaron emphasized that being subcontractors focusing on civil infrastructure places them at the project's foundation and finishing stages, which are critical for the success of subsequent mechanical and electrical works (07:24). Their work involves large, complex structures such as blast-resistant buildings and pipe racks, requiring high technical expertise and disciplined execution. Projects typically span 24 months, providing steady revenue streams and long-term client engagement. The company deliberately avoids projects perceived as "premium market giga projects" to stay within their expertise and ensure delivery excellence (05:51). This conservatism is driven by shareholder feedback to avoid market hype and focus on trusted EPC subcontracting roles. Aaron highlighted the cost of choosing cheap contractors, which often leads to delays, failures, and higher total costs, strengthening their value proposition despite perceptions of being more expensive (13:36). He stressed that delivering on safety, quality, and schedule justifies their pricing and builds reputation that EPCs respect. The company’s consistent record of delivery and client satisfaction reduces sales effort and solidifies repeat business.

Worker Welfare and Corporate Responsibility: Worker welfare is a core pillar of the company’s identity, contributing to its differentiation and award-winning reputation (28:49). Aaron shared that their worker welfare initiatives earned recognition such as the “Headphone Safety” award, reflecting their commitment to health and safety excellence (28:49). They invest heavily in camp management, focusing on culturally appropriate nourishment, rest, and well-being to sustain productivity and site safety (35:56). This off-site investment reduces accidents, increases morale, and improves overall operational outcomes. The company embraces external audits by EPCs and export credit agencies, which validate their compliance with strict labor and safety standards, helping them win and maintain contracts (30:24). Marcus and Aaron discussed collaborating with experts like Emma Seymour, a recognized leader in worker welfare, to scale and lobby for broader industry improvements (29:10). This aligns with a broader vision to raise standards in the built environment sector and influence client and government expectations. They foresee growing regulatory stringency around welfare and expect this to become a competitive differentiator in the Gulf and beyond.

Leadership Development and Industry Engagement: Leadership philosophy and humanizing leadership are core themes for future engagement and brand-building efforts (37:00). Marcus proposed launching a podcast series featuring leaders sharing personal stories, challenges, and lessons, focusing on authentic human experiences rather than company promotion (37:16). Aaron supported this, emphasizing the value of open conversations about leadership fears, mistakes, and successes to inspire the sector. The podcast would conclude with a “construction leadership playbook” capturing key quotes, advice, and best practices from guests. The two discussed the importance of inclusive leadership, with Aaron advocating a shift from diversity metrics to true inclusion, emphasizing culture and mindset over quotas (52:37). Aaron critiqued current DEI approaches, promoting an “I” for inclusion that covers diversity and equity naturally. Aaron shared his simple leadership mantras: “Always Be Closing (ABC), Keep Moving Forward (DMF), Question Everything Positively (QE), and Don’t Be An (DBAA)”, which guide operational and people leadership on site (39:32). This approach fosters open communication, safety, and respect across teams, reducing defensive behaviors and encouraging problem-solving. Both emphasized leadership humility, respect for workers, and maintaining focus on delivering value without ego.

Technology and Talent Acquisition Strategy: The company is leveraging technology and a unique recruitment strategy focused on deep candidate understanding and client alignment (00:00 - 00:30 and 55:00). Marcus described their proprietary system that maps leadership profiles against extensive market data on projects, companies, and stakeholders over the last 15 years, providing unmatched insights into candidate fit and market activity (02:23). This system integrates public data, project histories, and client relationships to identify ideal candidates and opportunities. Their recruitment process focuses on competency-based interviews aligned with client non-negotiables, often discarding traditional job descriptions to uncover true role needs (56:30). They guarantee candidate placements for six months, reflecting confidence in their vetting and alignment process. Marcus shared plans to expand into an advisory service offering heavy lifters for interim leadership roles, HR audits, digital transformation, and succession planning (58:49). This service responds to market demand for expert short-term interventions that stabilize and improve projects. Aaron expressed interest in these initiatives and agreed to review materials, with plans for joint discussions in Dubai to explore collaboration (58:32).

Industry Collaboration and Market Positioning: Building networks and promoting positive industry image are strategic priorities to enhance market presence and attract top talent (47:30). Marcus and Aaron discussed organizing a celebration of workspace designs to showcase innovation and improve the construction sector’s external reputation (48:55). This initiative aims to highlight creative, comfortable work environments that support retention and productivity. They noted the importance of evolving industry culture to attract and retain diverse talent through better environments and leadership approaches. Aaron shared experiences hosting clients and EPC partners onsite to expose them to worker realities, helping shift perceptions and build trust (44:45). Both leaders emphasized the need for patience and long-term relationship-building with major clients like OHI, recognizing that market entry and growth require sustained effort (52:42). The conversation concluded with mutual agreement to stay connected and explore collaboration opportunities, including knowledge sharing and leadership development.

sections.content: Building networks and promoting positive industry image are strategic priorities to enhance market presence and attract top talent (47:30). Marcus and Aaron discussed organizing a celebration of workspace designs to showcase innovation and improve the construction sector’s external reputation (48:55). This initiative aims to highlight creative, comfortable work environments that support retention and productivity. They noted the importance of evolving industry culture to attract and retain diverse talent through better environments and leadership approaches. Aaron shared experiences hosting clients and EPC partners onsite to expose them to worker realities, helping shift perceptions and build trust (44:45). Both leaders emphasized the need for patience and long-term relationship-building with major clients like OHI, recognizing that market entry and growth require sustained effort (52:42). The conversation concluded with mutual agreement to stay connected and explore collaboration opportunities, including knowledge sharing and leadership development.

Market Expansion: Successfully entered Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Abu Dhabi, focusing on civil construction products and sustainable growth.
Workforce Shift: Approximately 80% of workforce (5,000 employees) moved to Abu Dhabi, providing a 5-7 year project pipeline.
Client Philosophy: Emphasizes quality and trust over volume, specializing in civil infrastructure to ensure project success and client satisfaction.
Worker Welfare Recognition: Awarded for worker safety initiatives, highlighting the commitment to well-being and operational excellence.
Leadership Development: Plans to launch a podcast series to share authentic leadership stories and foster industry engagement.
Tech-Driven Recruitment: Utilizing proprietary systems for candidate fit by aligning skills with client needs, ensuring effective placements.
Notes
Middle East Market Expansion and Strategic Positioning
The company has strategically expanded into Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Abu Dhabi with a focused, controlled approach prioritizing core competencies and sustainable growth (04:35).
Aaron Hennessy explained that after 10 years of preparation, they simultaneously established operations in Saudi Arabia and Abu Dhabi to "get the headache over as quickly as possible" (05:51).
The entry targeted civil construction products only, avoiding speculative mega projects to maintain focus and quality.
Initial contracts were secured immediately through existing EPC relationships, including work with Technicas Renitas, GA Cinema, and Petrofect, emphasizing trusted partnerships.
The approach favors subcontracting roles under $1 billion, with a preference to start smaller (e.g., $100 million) to manage risk and learn site specifics before scaling up (08:54).
This method fosters deep embedding with clients, ensuring higher quality and more frequent payments, which contrasts with chasing large, risky contracts.
In terms of market differences, Aaron highlighted Oman’s slower decision-making culture and contractor mindset compared to Saudi and Abu Dhabi, where they found operations more aligned with their model (17:14).
Saudi faces challenges like limited talent, infrastructure gaps, and aggressive project deadlines, making it a tougher environment to scale quickly (19:09).
Operationally, logistics and labor laws are similar across Oman, Saudi, and UAE, allowing remote work and consistent processes despite geographic distances (20:47).
The company has shifted about 80% of its workforce (around 5,000 people) and resources to Abu Dhabi, where project visibility and pipeline extend 5 to 7 years, compared to a less predictable outlook in Oman and Saudi (26:58).
Abu Dhabi accounts for the majority of current work, followed by Saudi and then Oman, reflecting strategic prioritization based on market maturity and opportunities.
This shift aligns with a nomadic business model ready to pivot as market conditions evolve.
Operational Excellence and Client Relationship Philosophy
The company maintains a disciplined focus on quality, trust, and long-term client relationships over chasing volume or speculative growth (06:00).
Aaron emphasized that being subcontractors focusing on civil infrastructure places them at the project's foundation and finishing stages, which are critical for the success of subsequent mechanical and electrical works (07:24).
Their work involves large, complex structures such as blast-resistant buildings and pipe racks, requiring high technical expertise and disciplined execution.
Projects typically span 24 months, providing steady revenue streams and long-term client engagement.
The company deliberately avoids projects perceived as "premium market giga projects" to stay within their expertise and ensure delivery excellence (05:51).
This conservatism is driven by shareholder feedback to avoid market hype and focus on trusted EPC subcontracting roles.
Aaron highlighted the cost of choosing cheap contractors, which often leads to delays, failures, and higher total costs, strengthening their value proposition despite perceptions of being more expensive (13:36).
He stressed that delivering on safety, quality, and schedule justifies their pricing and builds reputation that EPCs respect.
The company’s consistent record of delivery and client satisfaction reduces sales effort and solidifies repeat business.
Worker Welfare and Corporate Responsibility
Worker welfare is a core pillar of the company’s identity, contributing to its differentiation and award-winning reputation (28:49).
Aaron shared that their worker welfare initiatives earned recognition such as the “Headphone Safety” award, reflecting their commitment to health and safety excellence (28:49).
They invest heavily in camp management, focusing on culturally appropriate nourishment, rest, and well-being to sustain productivity and site safety (35:56).
This off-site investment reduces accidents, increases morale, and improves overall operational outcomes.
The company embraces external audits by EPCs and export credit agencies, which validate their compliance with strict labor and safety standards, helping them win and maintain contracts (30:24).
Marcus and Aaron discussed collaborating with experts like Emma Seymour, a recognized leader in worker welfare, to scale and lobby for broader industry improvements (29:10).
This aligns with a broader vision to raise standards in the built environment sector and influence client and government expectations.
They foresee growing regulatory stringency around welfare and expect this to become a competitive differentiator in the Gulf and beyond.
Leadership Development and Industry Engagement
Leadership philosophy and humanizing leadership are core themes for future engagement and brand-building efforts (37:00).
Marcus proposed launching a podcast series featuring leaders sharing personal stories, challenges, and lessons, focusing on authentic human experiences rather than company promotion (37:16).
Aaron supported this, emphasizing the value of open conversations about leadership fears, mistakes, and successes to inspire the sector.
The podcast would conclude with a “construction leadership playbook” capturing key quotes, advice, and best practices from guests.
The two discussed the importance of inclusive leadership, with Aaron advocating a shift from diversity metrics to true inclusion, emphasizing culture and mindset over quotas (52:37).
Aaron critiqued current DEI approaches, promoting an “I” for inclusion that covers diversity and equity naturally.
Aaron shared his simple leadership mantras: “Always Be Closing (ABC), Keep Moving Forward (DMF), Question Everything Positively (QE), and Don’t Be An (DBAA)”, which guide operational and people leadership on site (39:32).
This approach fosters open communication, safety, and respect across teams, reducing defensive behaviors and encouraging problem-solving.
Both emphasized leadership humility, respect for workers, and maintaining focus on delivering value without ego.
Technology and Talent Acquisition Strategy
The company is leveraging technology and a unique recruitment strategy focused on deep candidate understanding and client alignment (00:00 - 00:30 and 55:00).
Marcus described their proprietary system that maps leadership profiles against extensive market data on projects, companies, and stakeholders over the last 15 years, providing unmatched insights into candidate fit and market activity (02:23).
This system integrates public data, project histories, and client relationships to identify ideal candidates and opportunities.
Their recruitment process focuses on competency-based interviews aligned with client non-negotiables, often discarding traditional job descriptions to uncover true role needs (56:30).
They guarantee candidate placements for six months, reflecting confidence in their vetting and alignment process.
Marcus shared plans to expand into an advisory service offering heavy lifters for interim leadership roles, HR audits, digital transformation, and succession planning (58:49).
This service responds to market demand for expert short-term interventions that stabilize and improve projects.
Aaron expressed interest in these initiatives and agreed to review materials, with plans for joint discussions in Dubai to explore collaboration (58:32).
Industry Collaboration and Market Positioning
Building networks and promoting positive industry image are strategic priorities to enhance market presence and attract top talent (47:30).
Marcus and Aaron discussed organizing a celebration of workspace designs to showcase innovation and improve the construction sector’s external reputation (48:55).
This initiative aims to highlight creative, comfortable work environments that support retention and productivity.
They noted the importance of evolving industry culture to attract and retain diverse talent through better environments and leadership approaches.
Aaron shared experiences hosting clients and EPC partners onsite to expose them to worker realities, helping shift perceptions and build trust (44:45).
Both leaders emphasized the need for patience and long-term relationship-building with major clients like OHI, recognizing that market entry and growth require sustained effort (52:42).
The conversation concluded with mutual agreement to stay connected and explore collaboration opportunities, including knowledge sharing and leadership development.

summary_bullets: GHD’s Recruitment Strategy: Focus on internal hiring, using external agencies only for specialized roles once or twice a year.
Taylor Sterling’s Expertise: A specialized executive search firm for the built environment, leveraging 25+ years of market experience and ethical standards.
Candidate-Centric Process: Emphasizes confidence-based interviewing, detailed candidate briefs, and deep analytical reports to enhance recruitment accuracy.
Transparent Fee Structure: Fees range from 16% to 20% of annual salary, with a retainer of 25% upfront and a six-month replacement guarantee.
Potential Collaboration: Agreement on partnership fit with GHD's recruitment goals, planning follow-up discussions to finalize terms and pilot engagements.
preferred_summary:
Client Relationship and Recruitment Strategy: The meeting confirmed GHD’s focus on internal hiring with selective external agency use, maintaining strong, long-term vendor relationships to ensure quality and fairness (08:55). Natalie Maiden outlined that GHD primarily fills roles internally, engaging agencies like Manassa and Partners only when specialized expertise is required, approximately once or twice a year (10:02). The Talent Acquisition (TA) team handles leadership roles up to business group leader, with executive searches reserved for the single regional general manager role (12:10). For roles difficult to fill internally, such as a recent business group leader for infrastructure and transport, GHD used external support, indicating openness to targeted agency partnerships (12:39). This approach limits volume but ensures quality and cultural fit, reflecting a strategic choice to build deep, trusted relationships with select recruiters rather than broad agency use.

Taylor Sterling’s Differentiated Recruitment Offering: Taylor Sterling positions itself as a highly specialized executive search firm for the built environment in the Middle East, with a focus on leadership roles and deep industry knowledge (15:01). Marcus Sterling shared their 25+ years of market experience and emphasized their strong ethical standards and tailored tech-driven approach, which includes a proprietary AI-powered recruitment platform developed since 2018 (14:45). The firm guarantees full confidentiality with encrypted data handling and conducts all initial meetings off-site to build trust, addressing common industry concerns around candidate privacy (20:45). They maintain a network of 150 top regional leaders through the OBE network, enabling access to exclusive talent pools unreachable by typical recruitment methods (20:46). Their process involves an 88-stage mapping and screening procedure using AI and data analytics to uncover candidates beyond standard platforms, resulting in a comprehensive short list of 3–5 candidates, improving match quality and reducing time-to-hire (24:12).

Process Excellence and Candidate Experience: Taylor Sterling emphasizes a candidate-centric process designed to enhance leadership recruitment outcomes and reduce client effort (25:40). The firm uses confidence-based interviewing and STAR techniques to assess competencies linked to client needs, improving evaluation accuracy and transparency (26:54). Candidates receive detailed briefs aligned with company culture and role requirements, helping them understand expectations and improving engagement (25:40). Clients receive deeply analyzed reports including DISC personality profiles, salary mapping, and motivation insights, eliminating the need to review traditional CVs and speeding decision-making (27:52). Natalie Maiden acknowledged the importance of elevating candidate experience at leadership levels, affirming the value of this detailed, respectful approach (28:48).

Commercial Terms and Partnership Potential: Taylor Sterling offers a transparent fee structure and flexible terms designed to build long-term partnerships aligned with client needs and market practices (30:49). Their fees range from 16% to 20% of annual salary, dependent on role complexity, with a typical retainer of 25% upfront and 50% on completion, including a six-month replacement guarantee (31:06). They reject contingency fees as outdated, instead sharing risk with clients and offering rebates and non-poaching protections to strengthen trust (31:52). Natalie Maiden expressed strong interest in reviewing the detailed fee breakdown and presentation, aiming to involve GHD’s global talent lead in Canada for final decisions, targeting a preliminary review around early February (7th–9th) (32:54). Marcus Sterling noted that once engaged, clients typically increase partnership scope due to demonstrated quality and ongoing monthly improvements of at least 5% efficiency gains in their recruitment process (30:29).

Strategic Alignment and Next Steps: Both parties agreed on the potential for collaboration, with Taylor Sterling’s offering fitting GHD’s selective, quality-focused recruitment strategy while promising better market positioning and time savings (13:06). Marcus Sterling proposed sharing an introductory brochure and case studies to demonstrate their market differentiation and candidate quality, which Natalie Maiden welcomed (18:40). Natalie plans to present the information to the broader talent team upon their return, setting up a follow-up conversation to explore engagement further (32:54). Marcus highlighted a near-term candidate ready for representation, offering a tailored fee arrangement outside standard terms, indicating flexibility and responsiveness to GHD’s needs (33:02). Both acknowledged the need for further detailed discussions to finalize partnership terms and begin pilot engagements aligned with GHD’s low-frequency, high-impact recruitment cycle.

GHD’s Recruitment Strategy: Focus on internal hiring, using external agencies only for specialized roles once or twice a year.
Taylor Sterling’s Expertise: A specialized executive search firm for the built environment, leveraging 25+ years of market experience and ethical standards.
Candidate-Centric Process: Emphasizes confidence-based interviewing, detailed candidate briefs, and deep analytical reports to enhance recruitment accuracy.
Transparent Fee Structure: Fees range from 16% to 20% of annual salary, with a retainer of 25% upfront and a six-month replacement guarantee.
Potential Collaboration: Agreement on partnership fit with GHD's recruitment goals, planning follow-up discussions to finalize terms and pilot engagements.
Notes
Client Relationship and Recruitment Strategy
The meeting confirmed GHD’s focus on internal hiring with selective external agency use, maintaining strong, long-term vendor relationships to ensure quality and fairness (08:55).
Natalie Maiden outlined that GHD primarily fills roles internally, engaging agencies like Manassa and Partners only when specialized expertise is required, approximately once or twice a year (10:02).
The Talent Acquisition (TA) team handles leadership roles up to business group leader, with executive searches reserved for the single regional general manager role (12:10).
For roles difficult to fill internally, such as a recent business group leader for infrastructure and transport, GHD used external support, indicating openness to targeted agency partnerships (12:39).
This approach limits volume but ensures quality and cultural fit, reflecting a strategic choice to build deep, trusted relationships with select recruiters rather than broad agency use.
Taylor Sterling’s Differentiated Recruitment Offering
Taylor Sterling positions itself as a highly specialized executive search firm for the built environment in the Middle East, with a focus on leadership roles and deep industry knowledge (15:01).
Marcus Sterling shared their 25+ years of market experience and emphasized their strong ethical standards and tailored tech-driven approach, which includes a proprietary AI-powered recruitment platform developed since 2018 (14:45).
The firm guarantees full confidentiality with encrypted data handling and conducts all initial meetings off-site to build trust, addressing common industry concerns around candidate privacy (20:45).
They maintain a network of 150 top regional leaders through the OBE network, enabling access to exclusive talent pools unreachable by typical recruitment methods (20:46).
Their process involves an 88-stage mapping and screening procedure using AI and data analytics to uncover candidates beyond standard platforms, resulting in a comprehensive short list of 3–5 candidates, improving match quality and reducing time-to-hire (24:12).
Process Excellence and Candidate Experience
Taylor Sterling emphasizes a candidate-centric process designed to enhance leadership recruitment outcomes and reduce client effort (25:40).
The firm uses confidence-based interviewing and STAR techniques to assess competencies linked to client needs, improving evaluation accuracy and transparency (26:54).
Candidates receive detailed briefs aligned with company culture and role requirements, helping them understand expectations and improving engagement (25:40).
Clients receive deeply analyzed reports including DISC personality profiles, salary mapping, and motivation insights, eliminating the need to review traditional CVs and speeding decision-making (27:52).
Natalie Maiden acknowledged the importance of elevating candidate experience at leadership levels, affirming the value of this detailed, respectful approach (28:48).
Commercial Terms and Partnership Potential
Taylor Sterling offers a transparent fee structure and flexible terms designed to build long-term partnerships aligned with client needs and market practices (30:49).
Their fees range from 16% to 20% of annual salary, dependent on role complexity, with a typical retainer of 25% upfront and 50% on completion, including a six-month replacement guarantee (31:06).
They reject contingency fees as outdated, instead sharing risk with clients and offering rebates and non-poaching protections to strengthen trust (31:52).
Natalie Maiden expressed strong interest in reviewing the detailed fee breakdown and presentation, aiming to involve GHD’s global talent lead in Canada for final decisions, targeting a preliminary review around early February (7th–9th) (32:54).
Marcus Sterling noted that once engaged, clients typically increase partnership scope due to demonstrated quality and ongoing monthly improvements of at least 5% efficiency gains in their recruitment process (30:29).
Strategic Alignment and Next Steps
Both parties agreed on the potential for collaboration, with Taylor Sterling’s offering fitting GHD’s selective, quality-focused recruitment strategy while promising better market positioning and time savings (13:06).
Marcus Sterling proposed sharing an introductory brochure and case studies to demonstrate their market differentiation and candidate quality, which Natalie Maiden welcomed (18:40).
Natalie plans to present the information to the broader talent team upon their return, setting up a follow-up conversation to explore engagement further (32:54).
Marcus highlighted a near-term candidate ready for representation, offering a tailored fee arrangement outside standard terms, indicating flexibility and responsiveness to GHD’s needs (33:02).
Both acknowledged the need for further detailed discussions to finalize partnership terms and begin pilot engagements aligned with GHD’s low-frequency, high-impact recruitment cycle.

summary_bullets: Business Growth: Aiming to double size this year through real estate and private equity, adding 15 new staff.
UK Joint Venture: £300 million project with Crown Prince of Dubai; majority ownership expected to finalize by May.
UAE Investments: Exploring $1 billion opportunity across six projects; potential to shift focus to Middle Eastern real estate.
New Private Equity Firm: Launching in Dubai by April, driven by a US investor; aims to integrate investments with development.
Leadership Restructuring: Hiring a COO within 6-12 months to allow focus on growth; prioritizing high-quality senior talent.
Confidential Recruitment: Strict NDAs to protect competitive advantage; emphasis on strategic hires and long-term partnerships with clients.
preferred_summary:
Business Growth and Strategic Expansion: The company is set to double its size this year by expanding into real estate development and private equity. Steven Coates detailed plans to double the business by the end of the year with a focus on real estate development investment (14:30) The expansion includes commercial and specification consulting, design management, and development projects led by different leaders. They forecast adding 15 new staff soon to support this growth while maintaining client selectivity and high-quality service. This growth phase reflects a shift from an established firm managing loyal clients to a more aggressive growth and investment model. The rationale is to leverage existing client trust and market position while diversifying into development and investment. Steven highlighted a £300 million UK development joint venture with the Crown Prince of Dubai, expected to finalize by May (11:10) The company will be the majority owner with the Crown Prince’s group as minority partners. This project represents a major milestone and will significantly increase their UK market footprint. The decision followed 18 months of paid negotiations, showing a strategic commitment to large-scale projects. It positions them competitively in both UK and Middle Eastern markets with high-profile partnerships. The firm is exploring a $1 billion investment opportunity in the UAE through To Buy Holdings across six projects (11:50) These investments remain tentative due to market volatility but could radically transform the business’s scale and focus. Steven is working closely with the board of To Buy Holdings to allocate funds strategically. This would pivot the company toward large-scale Middle Eastern real estate and infrastructure investments. The opportunity aligns with their vision of becoming a global player with diversified regional exposure. A new private equity business is launching in Dubai by April, driven by a wealthy US investor and facilitated by the chairman’s network (13:15) Steven will own this private equity firm, adding a new business line that complements real estate development. Lawyers are instructed, and the setup is underway, signaling a fast timeline and high priority. This diversification reflects a long-term vision to integrate investment and development under one umbrella. The chairman’s connections with billionaires and political figures add strategic weight and access to capital. Leadership restructuring is planned to support growth, including hiring a COO to take over Steven’s current role within 6 to 12 months (14:50) This will allow Steven to focus on development, investment, and private equity initiatives. The search for suitable senior talent is ongoing but challenging, showing the high bar set for leadership quality. The company also needs mid-level hires such as senior surveyors and project managers to manage daily operations. This transition is critical to sustaining rapid growth while preserving operational excellence.

Talent Acquisition and Confidentiality: Talent growth is essential but tightly controlled to protect competitive advantage and client confidentiality. Steven emphasized the need for discretion around recruitment plans, requesting strict confidentiality agreements with Marcus (09:50) He highlighted the sensitivity of the 15 new hires and strategic hires like the COO. Confidentiality is crucial due to competitive risks and overlapping industry relationships. Steven trusts Marcus but remains cautious given Marcus’s network and mutual contacts like Chris Cooper. This caution reflects a culture of protecting strategic moves and client relationships carefully. Marcus reassured confidentiality by explaining strict NDAs with all clients and candidates, positioning it as protection for all parties (16:40) He clarified that their involvement often reaches strategic succession planning and executive-level replacements. This approach differentiates their service from more casual recruitment firms and aligns with Steven’s need for discretion. Marcus highlighted their focus on long-term partnerships and strategic alignment with clients’ business goals. He underscored their professionalism and boundaries, avoiding informal socializing to maintain trust. Marcus described their process as deeply strategic, working with clients at the board level to define goals and timelines (16:55) This aligns with Steven’s emphasis on selective client engagement and high-quality outcomes. Their model supports complex hires needed for scaling businesses like Steven’s firm. The strategic focus helps handle sensitive market moves and competitive challenges effectively. This process supports the company’s goal of expanding without losing control or leaking plans.

Industry Network Development and Brand Building: Building a strong industry network and community is a priority to support growth and reputation. Marcus shared progress on a professional network with 150 members, targeting 250 by year-end, focused on developers and subcontractors (17:30) The network hosts steering committees and roundtables to foster collaboration and knowledge sharing. They plan to launch a podcast by the end of the quarter to further humanize the brand and engage the community. Collaboration with key figures like Cynthia, who works with the UK government, aims to strengthen influence and sourcing capabilities. This initiative creates a pipeline of talent and partnerships aligned with Steven’s growth ambitions. Steven expressed strong support for Marcus’s network efforts, recognizing their potential to attract quality people and energy (18:20) He highlighted Marcus’s credibility and the positive impression he makes within the industry. This network will indirectly support Steven’s recruitment and business development efforts. The synergy between network growth and business expansion is a strategic asset. Both see this as a long-term investment in ecosystem building rather than short-term hiring.

Operational Challenges and Market Positioning: The company balances operational needs with strategic confidentiality amid competitive pressures. Steven acknowledged difficulty finding the right senior candidates and the need to replace his role to focus on new ventures (14:40) This reflects growing pains of a maturing firm transitioning from founder-led to professional management. The challenge underlines the competitive market for high-caliber leadership in real estate and investment sectors. It also indicates the company’s ambition to scale sustainably by upgrading organizational structure. The process is ongoing with support from Marcus’s firm for strategic hires. Steven is wary of overlapping industry relationships, especially involving Chris Cooper and Pascal’s group, highlighting competitive sensitivity (15:20) This wariness influences partnership and recruitment decisions to avoid conflicts or information leaks. It shows the importance of trust and clear boundaries in their market segment. Managing these relationships carefully protects the company’s reputation and client trust. This approach fits with their selective client engagement and premium brand positioning. Marcus’s firm’s focus on strategic succession and replacement helps counter payment issues and operational risks common in other firms (14:40) Their high-touch, strategic approach reduces hiring risks and enhances long-term stability for clients. This aligns with Steven’s experience of selective client management and reliable partnerships. The partnership between the two firms aims to embed this operational robustness during expansion. It forms part of the company’s broader risk management and quality assurance framework.

sections.heading: Operational Challenges and Market Positioning
sections.content: The company balances operational needs with strategic confidentiality amid competitive pressures. Steven acknowledged difficulty finding the right senior candidates and the need to replace his role to focus on new ventures (14:40) This reflects growing pains of a maturing firm transitioning from founder-led to professional management. The challenge underlines the competitive market for high-caliber leadership in real estate and investment sectors. It also indicates the company’s ambition to scale sustainably by upgrading organizational structure. The process is ongoing with support from Marcus’s firm for strategic hires. Steven is wary of overlapping industry relationships, especially involving Chris Cooper and Pascal’s group, highlighting competitive sensitivity (15:20) This wariness influences partnership and recruitment decisions to avoid conflicts or information leaks. It shows the importance of trust and clear boundaries in their market segment. Managing these relationships carefully protects the company’s reputation and client trust. This approach fits with their selective client engagement and premium brand positioning. Marcus’s firm’s focus on strategic succession and replacement helps counter payment issues and operational risks common in other firms (14:40) Their high-touch, strategic approach reduces hiring risks and enhances long-term stability for clients. This aligns with Steven’s experience of selective client management and reliable partnerships. The partnership between the two firms aims to embed this operational robustness during expansion. It forms part of the company’s broader risk management and quality assurance framework.

summary_bullets: Leadership Network Launch: Approximately 130–140 senior P&L leaders in built environment collaborating on industry challenges since May last year.
Annual Events Scheduled: Three to four main events, including roundtables on contract incentives and risk sharing, planned to deepen engagement.
Talent Pipeline Crisis: Built environment graduates declined from 3.1% to 2.8%; 65–70% leadership shortfall projected in five to seven years.
Contract Reform Needed: Current contract models disadvantage weaker parties, increasing risk and project delays; reform essential to retain talent.
Strategic Collaborations Forming: Backing from major institutions to align efforts for systemic changes in talent acquisition and project delivery.
Membership Growth Target: Network aims to increase membership to 250 senior leaders, maintaining quality while enhancing influence and collaboration.
preferred_summary:
Built Environment Network Development: The network Marcus Sterling has built aims to unite senior P&L leaders across developers, consultants, and contractors to solve industry challenges collaboratively. Marcus Sterling launched a leadership network with about 130–140 members focused on built environment issues by May last year (22:00) The group includes mainly senior P&L leaders from contractors, consultants, and developers committed to open collaboration. Marcus emphasized confidentiality and trust as core values that differentiate the network. The network uses a WhatsApp group with strict guidelines to maintain focus and civility. The goal is to foster free discussion on talent, risk-sharing, and industry sustainability, avoiding ego-driven events. The network plans three to four main events plus social gatherings annually to deepen engagement (22:11) Upcoming events include roundtables on contract incentives and risk sharing, with pilot projects planned. The next steering group meeting is set for Friday with influential industry leaders. Events will be held in notable venues like the new Aegis Auditorium to attract high-profile participation. Marcus aims to humanize leadership through a podcast launching by end of Q2, featuring candid industry conversations. The group targets improving the industry’s talent pipeline by addressing leadership deficits and engagement (24:00) Industry data shows a decline in built environment graduates from 3.1% to 2.8% recently, with projections of a 65–70% leadership shortfall in five to seven years. Marcus highlighted lack of awareness in schools and universities as a key barrier to recruitment. Efforts target grassroots education to attract new talent by promoting the industry’s long-term impact and global opportunities. The network’s collective expertise is seen as critical to reversing the talent drain and improving industry health. Chris Jones confirmed Jensen Hughes’ interest and capacity to contribute given their regional leadership and size (27:30) Jensen Hughes employs about 1800 globally, with 180 people in the Middle East and 25 in India, expanding into new regions. Their strong ties to civil defense authorities and involvement in giga projects like Qiddiya and NEOM position them as key industry players. Jones noted their move towards higher-value sectors such as rail, aviation, and oil & gas, which offer better contract terms and influence. Jensen Hughes is ready to add value to the network’s efforts on leadership and industry collaboration.

Contract Health and Industry Challenges: The network and Jensen Hughes both recognize contract structures and risk sharing as major issues that must be reformed to attract talent and improve collaboration. Current contract models often disadvantage weaker parties, adding risk and slowing project delivery as Chris Jones explained (28:00) Jensen Hughes operates mostly as a subconsultant with limited control over contract terms, affecting fee stability. They avoid contracts with unlimited liabilities, choosing to walk away rather than accept unfair terms. The firm strives to work in sectors where they can negotiate better terms and reduce risk exposure. These contract pressures contribute to industry stress and talent loss, reinforcing the need for network-driven reform. Marcus Sterling’s research focuses on sharing incentives and reducing penalties to improve cooperation and claims management (23:30) The network is studying successful models from Norway’s oil and aviation sectors to inform local pilots. Discussions include how to keep claims professionals constructive and reduce adversarial behaviors. The network aims to pilot contract frameworks that encourage collaboration and attract future talent. This approach aligns with broader goals to make the UAE a global leader in healthy industry practices.

Strategic Industry Positioning and Vision: Both leaders see the network and Jensen Hughes as pivotal to shaping a sustainable and innovative future for the Middle East built environment. Marcus Sterling envisions the network as a platform for frank leadership dialogue and genuine change (18:00) The network rejects ego-driven recognition and emphasizes real impact and accountability. He is committed to improving industry conditions before retiring in four to five years. The group’s invite-only, Chatham House framework encourages open, honest conversations. Marcus’s approach is to call out poor practices while nurturing collaborative solutions. Chris Jones emphasized Jensen Hughes’ market leadership and growth strategy to support this vision (27:30) Jensen Hughes leads globally in safety and security with a workforce seven times larger than closest competitors. Recent expansion into India and strong relationships with civil defense position them for growth. Their reputation on key giga projects underlines their influence in shaping industry standards. Jones sees collaboration with the network as a way to extend their leadership and contribute to industry health. The network seeks to influence broader industry organizations and professional bodies to unify efforts (15:00) Backing was secured from RIBA, ICE, CIOB, RICS, CIPS, CIPD, and others to align stakeholders. This coalition supports tackling systemic problems across consulting, contracting, and development. The collective voice aims to push for meaningful reform in contracts, talent, and project delivery. Such alignment enhances credibility and impact of pilot programs and policy advocacy.

Operational and Engagement Improvements: The network is evolving operationally to maintain engagement, manage scale, and maximize impact through targeted events and communication. Strict group guidelines and curated member lists maintain focus and prevent distractions in communications (33:30) The WhatsApp group limits off-topic chatter and controls recruitment introductions via Marcus. The directory of 154 members is actively updated to include only senior P&L decision-makers. Members represent heavy hitters across HR, delivery, and commercial functions, ensuring diverse perspectives. This controlled environment helps build trust and keeps discussions productive. Future plans include splinter groups and thematic breakfasts to deepen topical discussions (22:00) Smaller focused sessions will address specific industry challenges like leadership gaps or contract reforms. Social events serve to build relationships and reduce silos between competing firms. The podcast will add a new channel for storytelling and leadership humanization. These steps help translate network energy into concrete business outcomes and cultural shifts. The network’s referral program and recruitment advisory service support talent acquisition (36:00) Marcus offers a referral scheme with rates across the network to incentivize leadership recruitment. The advisory side launched mid-year provides tailored strategic advice on leadership hiring. This integrated approach strengthens the network’s value proposition to members and partners. Chris Jones expressed interest in leveraging these capabilities for Jensen Hughes’ growth. The network plans to grow membership to 250 senior leaders to enhance influence (33:45) Current members include notable figures from Atkins, SSH, Rambo, and other leading firms. Growth is deliberate to maintain quality and commitment to collaboration. Increasing scale will improve reach for pilot initiatives and policy influence. Marcus controls onboarding tightly to preserve the group’s ethos and effectiveness.

title: Recruitment Strategy and Service Offering
transcript:
Marcus aims to humanize leadership through a podcast launching by end of Q2, featuring candid industry conversations.
The group targets improving the industry’s talent pipeline by addressing leadership deficits and engagement (24:00)
Industry data shows a decline in built environment graduates from 3.1% to 2.8% recently, with projections of a 65–70% leadership shortfall in five to seven years.
Marcus highlighted lack of awareness in schools and universities as a key barrier to recruitment.
Efforts target grassroots education to attract new talent by promoting the industry’s long-term impact and global opportunities.
The network’s collective expertise is seen as critical to reversing the talent drain and improving industry health.
Chris Jones confirmed Jensen Hughes’ interest and capacity to contribute given their regional leadership and size (27:30)
Jensen Hughes employs about 1800 globally, with 180 people in the Middle East and 25 in India, expanding into new regions.
Their strong ties to civil defense authorities and involvement in giga projects like Qiddiya and NEOM position them as key industry players.
Jones noted their move towards higher-value sectors such as rail, aviation, and oil & gas, which offer better contract terms and influence.
Jensen Hughes is ready to add value to the network’s efforts on leadership and industry collaboration.
Contract Health and Industry Challenges
The network and Jensen Hughes both recognize contract structures and risk sharing as major issues that must be reformed to attract talent and improve collaboration.
Current contract models often disadvantage weaker parties, adding risk and slowing project delivery as Chris Jones explained (28:00)
Jensen Hughes operates mostly as a subconsultant with limited control over contract terms, affecting fee stability.
They avoid contracts with unlimited liabilities, choosing to walk away rather than accept unfair terms.
The firm strives to work in sectors where they can negotiate better terms and reduce risk exposure.
These contract pressures contribute to industry stress and talent loss, reinforcing the need for network-driven reform.
Marcus Sterling’s research focuses on sharing incentives and reducing penalties to improve cooperation and claims management (23:30)
The network is studying successful models from Norway’s oil and aviation sectors to inform local pilots.
Discussions include how to keep claims professionals constructive and reduce adversarial behaviors.
The network aims to pilot contract frameworks that encourage collaboration and attract future talent.
This approach aligns with broader goals to make the UAE a global leader in healthy industry practices.

Both leaders see the network and Jensen Hughes as pivotal to shaping a sustainable and innovative future for the Middle East built environment.
Marcus Sterling envisions the network as a platform for frank leadership dialogue and genuine change (18:00)
The network rejects ego-driven recognition and emphasizes real impact and accountability.
He is committed to improving industry conditions before retiring in four to five years.
The group’s invite-only, Chatham House framework encourages open, honest conversations.
Marcus’s approach is to call out poor practices while nurturing collaborative solutions.
Chris Jones emphasized Jensen Hughes’ market leadership and growth strategy to support this vision (27:30)

summary_bullets: Business Growth Focus: Growth in UAE driven by volume recruitment, with fewer external leadership hires.
Client Activity Shift: Client engagement moved from a 70-30 to 60-40 split favoring UAE, enhancing future business.
Internal Promotion Strategy: Recruitment emphasizes internal promotions over agency use, aiming for stability and reduced costs.
Operational Enhancements: Competency-based interviews and data usage improve candidate matching and client satisfaction.
Future Initiatives: Plans for 2024 include expanding OB network and launching a podcast, targeting high-quality client engagement.
Personal Impacts on Leadership: Executives face personal transitions, affecting availability but maintaining strategic business focus.
preferred_summary:
Business Growth and Market Position: The company is experiencing significant growth in the UAE, driven by volume recruitment and internal networking rather than targeted leadership hires (07:34). Alejandro Garcia Vinagre reports that the main driver of growth is volume hiring, with recruitment runs overseas supplementing internal networks. Leadership roles have seen less external recruitment, with key positions filled internally, as in the recent replacement of an MD role (16:48). This growth focus on volume rather than niche leadership roles reflects a strategic decision aligned with current market demand and company capability. The shift of client activity from Saudi Arabia from a 70-30 split to a 60-40 favoring UAE positions the company well for future business consolidation (11:50). The company is building deeper client relationships and refining delivery models to enhance competitive positioning (12:50). The adoption of competency-based interviewing and tailored DISC analysis reflects efforts to improve candidate fit and service quality. The goal is to become the top data-driven recruitment firm in the region by the end of the year, aiming to leverage data for scalability and value creation. Relationships in Saudi Arabia remain strong despite limited activity, allowing quick re-engagement when market conditions improve. This approach addresses competitive pressure by focusing on quality and client alignment rather than volume alone.

Talent Acquisition and Recruitment Strategy: Recruitment efforts prioritize internal promotions and volume hiring, limiting agency involvement for now (15:00). Alejandro confirms no new agency contracts have been signed for months, reflecting a deliberate internal focus. The company tested external and internal candidate streams for a leadership role and chose internal promotion for stability and fit (16:48). This strategy reduces reliance on external vendors and aims to build long-term internal capacity. The internal focus also helps control recruitment costs and accelerates hiring cycles. Marcus Taylor Sterling highlights a recent unsuccessful agency partnership due to lack of engagement and delivery (14:50). Despite producing a comprehensive candidate list, their team never received feedback or approval to proceed with delivery. This experience underscores the importance of clear communication and alignment between agency and client expectations. Marcus stresses that strong networks exist but are underutilized, suggesting better collaboration could improve results. This insight may encourage the company to revisit external partnerships once internal capacity is optimized.

Operational Improvements and Delivery Model: Significant enhancements have been made to the operational delivery model focusing on structured candidate assessment and data use (12:50). Marcus describes integration of competency-based interviewing across key areas: growth, risk, compliance, capability, and capacity. Customizing DISC personality analysis for the industry is improving candidate matching accuracy. These changes aim to reduce hiring risks and improve client satisfaction by delivering better-fit candidates. The company’s renewed emphasis on data aims to support scalability and measurable performance improvements throughout the year.

Strategic Initiatives and Future Planning: The company is launching new initiatives to expand reach and deepen market engagement in 2024 (10:10). Plans include doubling the size of the OB network and launching a podcast by the end of the first quarter, featuring industry leaders like Campbell Grays and Jason Morris. A steering committee meeting is scheduled for Friday to finalize topics for the next major event, demonstrating structured planning and stakeholder involvement. Growth focus is on high-quality client acquisition and targeted engagement rather than broad geographic expansion, particularly avoiding insecure markets like Saudi Arabia currently. These efforts aim to solidify brand presence and build sustainable community engagement for longer-term growth.

Leadership and Personal Context Impacting Business: Both executives balance demanding roles with significant personal life transitions impacting availability and focus (20:00). Marcus plans to relocate his family to South Africa this summer due to lifestyle and family needs, aiming for a flexible work arrangement with regular travel between locations. Alejandro is managing a personal move in the current month, limiting networking and availability temporarily. Both acknowledge the emotional challenges of work-life balance, especially related to parenting and long-term commitments. These personal factors may influence scheduling and availability but do not diminish strategic business focus or leadership effectiveness.

preferred_summary:
Recruitment Progress and Candidate Pipeline: The team secured four highly qualified candidates ready for interviews next week, marking a strong recruitment milestone amid a challenging hiring market (27:01). They started with a longlist of 20 candidates, which was refined to 13, of whom nine engaged positively, and finally four candidates completed full screening, an above-average success given the foreign market context. Marcus highlighted the rarity and quality of these candidates for an emerging company in a new country, emphasizing the value of this pipeline for the client’s growth. The candidates include a top-tier engineer scoring 83 on competency metrics, a strong Italian female candidate, and a South African currently in Melbourne, all showing genuine interest and cultural fit. Nigel noted that one candidate, Damien, has already joined another company but is on one-week notice, providing potential quick availability. The team will conduct initial 30-minute character-fit interviews next week, followed by more technical conversations, ensuring a thorough vetting process before final decisions.

Client Demand and Market Conditions: Recruitment demand remains high but volatile, with clients issuing urgent requests for large numbers of profiles by December, creating pressure on capacity and delivery timelines (05:57). Marcus explained clients are increasingly concerned with succession planning and growth, leading to more active candidate engagement and sensitivity to retention risks. Daniel described a recruitment scenario involving a long-term but initially low-volume project, easing immediate pressure but requiring sustained quality hires. The team is cautious about over-promising, emphasizing the importance of managing client expectations around capacity, with a current delivery rate capped at four to five hires per month. Marcus stressed the strategic value of saying “no” to overloaded demands to maintain quality and avoid burnout, reflecting on a recent client who requested 12 hires urgently but was offered a realistic monthly capacity instead.

Candidate Engagement and Communication Strategy: The recruitment process uses a multi-stage, personalized outreach approach combining social messaging, emails, calls, and WhatsApp to connect with typically busy and less active professionals (13:44). Marcus outlined the staged communication method designed to build rapport without overwhelming candidates, proven to increase engagement despite taking more time. The candidate pool exhibited lower-than-normal dropout rates during initial screening, indicating strong interest and effective outreach tailored to individual motivations. Feedback and analytics from candidate responses were actively used to refine messaging and prioritize those showing genuine interest and cultural fit. The team balanced confidentiality with transparency by encrypting candidate reports and sharing detailed background, salary expectations, and motivations to help clients quickly assess fit.

Interview Scheduling and Next Steps: The team requested client availability for interview scheduling next week, aiming to complete initial screenings before Christmas to maximize candidate responsiveness and secure timely hires (25:34). Marcus asked clients to arrange interviews with all four shortlisted candidates, emphasizing the importance of these initial conversations to assess cultural fit. Nigel added that one candidate based in Melbourne will transit through Dubai before Christmas, enabling a potential face-to-face meeting, which may enhance candidate assessment. Craig confirmed plans to review diaries and accommodate interviews despite upcoming travel, noting the client’s understanding of holiday-related scheduling challenges. Marcus committed to promptly sending encrypted candidate reports with passwords following the meeting to maintain confidentiality and streamline the process.

Client Resource and Event Updates: The team is managing internal resource constraints and external event sponsorship challenges while maintaining recruitment momentum (00:00). Marcus reported having over 50 confirmed attendees for an upcoming Christmas event but currently no sponsors secured, highlighting a gap in funding that could affect event execution. He is following up with finance to clarify outstanding sponsorship commitments ahead of the end-of-month payroll deadline. Despite these pressures, Marcus remains focused on delivering recruitment outcomes and balancing operational priorities, indicating resilience and adaptability within the team.

sections.heading: Candidate Profiling and Technology Integration
sections.content: The firm’s use of AI and data analytics is central to delivering high-quality candidate shortlists and improving hiring outcomes. Marcus explained their AI approach combines competency-based analysis, social footprint evaluation, and project involvement cross-checking to identify candidates often overlooked by conventional means (00:29). For example, in bridge engineering, they analyzed project timelines and publications alongside candidate employment history to uncover hidden talents. DISC behavioral profiling of candidates’ digital footprints helps identify leadership and client engagement potential beyond job titles, enhancing match quality. The candidate evaluation involves a multi-step interview process including a 30-40 minute first call focusing on motivations and non-negotiables, all conducted confidentially before disclosing client details (00:27). Follow-up interviews deepen competency assessment using STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) methodology, scored against six key competencies including strategic mindset, client safety, and operational management (00:34, 00:38). Their candidate dossiers include personalized leadership briefs tailored to each candidate’s background and the role’s specifics to enhance engagement and cultural fit (00:36). Salary benchmarking covers all total compensation components such as housing, education allowances, and bonuses to provide transparency and support offer negotiations (00:39). The process culminates in a shortlist of 3 to 5 candidates out of an initial long list of ~20, with real-time tracking of progress through to offer acceptance (00:32).
